Requires two processors.","kind":"orderable","skins":{"db9":"teal"}}},"datasheet":{"sha256":"ef631c21f0ccd007f5d3eac2ccce2af9b9ca557ba58e153c09f7471bacb9404f","title":"Dell EMC PowerEdge R740xd Spec Sheet"},"description":"2U two-socket rack server - 24 x 2.5 inch front drive bays","format":1,"gaps":[{"note":"dell/riser-divider-plate-14g@1's OUTLINE AND DEPTH ARE MEASURED and its FACE IS NOT. Both bodies come off Dell's service model to the hundredth - face 267.32..278.64 and 297.10..308.42, y 1.81..42.42, 17.61 proud - but what is printed or punched on them has not been established from any figure. Riser 1's equivalent plate carries a five-slot column that appears in no cut of the model at any plane and had to be read off ISM figure 8; whether these two carry the same column, or anything else, was NOT SEARCHED FOR rather than looked for and found absent. The recess drawn for the card clip is drawn because a clip sits in a recess on riser 1, not because this plate was seen to have one.","reason":"needs-photo","scope":["rear"],"wanted":"a rear photograph or ISM figure at usable resolution across face 267..309, which would settle both plates at once - they are the same pressing","what":"riser-divider-plate-face-detail-unknown"},{"note":"WHICH OF THE TWO IS IN FRONT IS ASSERTED, NOT MEASURED. dell/riser-1-top- shelf-14g@1 is 14.68 proud (measured, the chassis shell's front) and dell/riser-1-shroud-14g@1's plate is extruded at 17.76 (an approximation across a whole outline, as that file's depth key says), so the plate drew in front and the shelf read as tucked under the piece it closes the top of. The operator, looking at the render against the hardware, says the shelf is the outermost thing there. It is expressed as a 3.10 `lift` on the composition - the smallest value that clears 17.76 - so both measured depths survive untouched and only the ordering changes. If the plate's width and depth are ever settled properly (see riser-1-shroud-rib-width-unresolved, which is the same piece of missing evidence) this lift should be re-derived rather than kept.","reason":"needs-hardware","scope":["rear"],"wanted":"a mechanical drawing or a caliper on the hardware giving the riser-1 shroud plate's front and the chassis top shelf's front at the same face x, which is the one measurement that settles the ordering outright","what":"riser-1-shelf-over-plate-ordering-estimated"},{"note":"THE MID BAYS ARE NOT NUMBERED HERE, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. This device numbers its front drives 0 to 23 and its rear drives 12 to 15 or 24 to 27, in both cases because Dell's own label says so and the numbering was checked against it. NOTHING FOUND SO FAR SAYS WHAT DELL CALLS THE FOUR MID-BAY DRIVES. They are `mid-lff-0..3` and `mid-sff-0..3`, which are positions and not claims: they say \"the four slots, left to right\" and assert nothing about what the machine prints or what iDRAC reports. Inventing a range that looked like the others - 24 to 27 say - would have been the easy thing and would have been a fabrication of exactly the kind the front and rear numbering was careful to avoid.","reason":"vendor-silent","scope":["top"],"wanted":"the mid-drive-tray page of the R740xd installation and service manual, or a photograph of the tray with its silkscreen legible","what":"mid-bay-drive-numbering-unknown"},{"note":"THE PREVIOUS FORM OF THIS GAP SAID THE CAD POSE WAS EXPLODED. IT IS NOT, AND THE SENTENCE IS KEPT HERE BECAUSE IT IS THE INSTRUCTIVE PART. A reading of R740XD_GPU_Brackets_01-1 was rejected on the grounds that its y extent ran -40 to +24 against an 86.8 mm panel - \"not a seated pose\". That was a Y-CONVENTION ARTEFACT IN THE READER, not a fact about the model. Calibrated against the rear handle, whose device y is trusted, the convention is face_y = 86.8 - raw_y; it reproduces the handle's low edge at 42.35 to the hundredth and this assembly's own sibling R740XD_Expansioncard_Clip-1.001 at y 1.81..44.81, the figure riser-1-shroud-14g already carried from an independent read. The pose is seated and the 36.9 mm was real all along - a plausibility check that fires on the reader instead of the data rejects good evidence, and it cost a wrong fix at the other end of the part. WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SHOWS, descended to mesh children, is two levels: Body_2_3.002 at 111.70..148.60, 11.06 proud - a wide lower shelf, now drawn - and Body_1_3.005 at 125.00..135.10, 17.71 proud - a narrow rib. WHAT IS STILL OPEN is the rib. riser-1-shroud-14g draws it 120.64..137.26, about 4 mm wider on each side than the body at that depth. The outline came from cad-outline.py cutting at the panel plane, which returns the SILHOUETTE of everything the plane crosses rather than one body, so it cannot settle a single body's width. Re-cutting it would move the slot column and the clip recess, both photo-measured off ISM figure 8 and both currently agreeing with the render, so it is recorded rather than guessed.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["rear"],"wanted":"a mechanical drawing of the riser-1 shroud, or a clean section of R740XD_GPU_Brackets_01-1 above the shelf, to settle the raised rib's width independently of the panel-plane silhouette","what":"riser-1-shroud-rib-width-unresolved"},{"note":"THE NUMBER CAME FROM A DESCRIPTION, NOT A MEASUREMENT. std/vga@1 stands 6.73 proud because that is what a D-sub does when its flange bolts through sheet metal, and on this machine's front the connector is on the control panel board, which sits back from the bezel - so only a little of it emerges. The operator, looking at the hardware, put that at \"a millimetre and a half\"; `inset: 5.23` is 6.73 less 1.50 and is therefore an estimate dressed as two decimal places. IT IS THE SETBACK THAT IS UNKNOWN, not the connector. The 6.73 is TE 114-40010's mating dimension and stays; what nobody here has measured is how far behind the faceplate the board sits. A caliper on the hardware, or any drawing that dimensions the control panel board against the front bezel, replaces one number and nothing else. THE REAR D-SUBS ARE NOT AFFECTED. g.data-description: the power button - what you press, not what you plug into
g.title: power-btn

g.data-description: the power symbol itself, lit from behind. It is the glyph that lights, not a separate indicator beside it, which is why the element is the symbol's own box rather than a dot.

the front I/O: two USB 2.0, the iDRAC Direct micro USB and the VGA. Three families in one block DELIBERATELY - Dell's own table calls them one thing, the right control panel, and they do one job: they are what you plug a keyboard, a screen and a laptop into when you are standing at the rack. Splitting them by media would draw three groups where the faceplate has one. None of them is traffic; this chassis carries no network port on its front face.
g.title: usb-1

g.data-description: printed and moulded marks that say what the opening beside them is for. They are `furniture` because nothing plugs into them and nothing lights - a mark that lit would be a lamp, and this panel has one of those and it is the power button.
g.title: mark-usb-1

g.title: panel-grid

g.data-description: ISM table 8 entire. `connected` is "solid green for two seconds" - a laptop or tablet has been plugged in, and the two seconds is how long that indication lasts before the next one rather than a blink, so it is modelled solid and the duration recorded here instead of being invented as a rate. `recognised` is "flashing green (on for two seconds and off for two seconds)", which is 0.25 Hz exactly. `off` is the device unplugged.
g.title: idrac-direct-led

g.data-description: the rack release rockers, one built into each ear. Pressed to free the chassis from the rail so it can be drawn out - so they are pressed, but they release the BOX rather than operating anything in it, which is why they are furniture and not `mgmt`.
g.title: latch-left

rect.data-description: the pressed face at the top of the rocker, where the finger goes. Below it the moulding is a plain grip.

g.data-description: the rack release rockers, one built into each ear. Pressed to free the chassis from the rail so it can be drawn out - so they are pressed, but they release the BOX rather than operating anything in it, which is why they are furniture and not `mgmt`.
g.title: latch-right

rect.data-description: the pressed face at the top of the rocker, where the finger goes. Below it the moulding is a plain grip.

g.data-description: the drive glyph, lit. ISM table 4 - solid amber if there is a drive error.
the thermometer glyph. Solid amber on a thermal error - ambient out of range, or a fan failure.
the lightning glyph. Solid amber on voltage out of range, a failed PSU or a failed voltage regulator.
the memory glyph. Solid amber on a memory error.
the PCIe glyph. Solid amber when a PCIe card errors.

rect.data-description: the system health and system ID bar, and the button that switches between the two modes. ISM table 5 in full: solid blue - on, healthy, ID mode not active; blinking blue - ID mode active; solid amber - fail-safe mode; blinking amber - a fault, check the event log. NO RATE IS PUBLISHED for either blink, so 1 Hz is this library's reading and is not a figure Dell states - unlike the drive lamp, where the article gives twice and four times a second and the model carries them.

rect.data-states: off ready transfer updating disabled fail-safe unresponsive
rect.data-description: the iDRAC Quick Sync 2 bar, and the button that turns the feature on and off. Every code in ISM table 6, at the shape that table gives. `disabled` IS WHY THE SEQUENCE MECHANISM EXISTS: Dell's wording is 'blinks white five times rapidly and then turns off', which is five on-phases, five off-phases and a long dark tail - a pattern no colour and rate can say. The 2.5 second tail is this library's reading of 'and then turns off'; the five blinks are Dell's own count.

g.data-description: removable covers over the face. The bezel is the only one, and it is DRAWN BY DEFAULT AND TAKEN OFF IN THE VIEWER - which is a reversal, and the reason is worth keeping. It was `optional: bezel` before, meaning the build dropped it unless asked for it by name. The argument was that it hides the drives it protects, so the default drawing should leave it off. That is a fair thing to want and it was the wrong mechanism for it: `optional` excludes a part from the ARTIFACT, so nothing downstream could put it back. A machine that ships with a bezel rendered as one that has none, in every consumer, with no way to ask. The kit already had the right control. `behaviour: mounts` puts a pull handle on any cover - "take off this cover to see behind it" - and it drives 2D and 3D alike. So the bezel is placed like any other part and the drives are one click away, which is the same gesture the top panel uses and one fewer concept than it had.
